title: Tending the garden

segments.voice: Yesterday, yes means yes: Jesus folding oaths and ordinary speech into one kind of truth. Your line was plain truth. Did you keep the promise you named, and did any I swear slip out? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

A plastic bag snagged on a fence by the bus stop, flapping in the wind. Everybody walks past it. It isn't anybody's bag, so it isn't anybody's job. Now go back to the second chapter of the Bible. There's no city yet, no bus stop, no fence. There's a garden, and one human being, and before anything else goes wrong, God gives that human a job. Not a title. Not a throne. A job, with dirt under the fingernails. Today: tending the garden.

Here's the verse, Genesis 2:15, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." Dress it and keep it. Two verbs. Readers of the Hebrew point out that the first is a word for working the ground that elsewhere also means to serve. The second, they note, means to keep, to guard, to watch over, and it's used for keeping God's commandments. So the human is placed in the garden as a gardener who serves it and a guard who protects it. Not an owner. A psalm makes the ownership plain: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." Christians read the first chapter of Genesis too, where humans are given dominion over the creatures. Some readers once took dominion as permission to use things up. Others, reading it beside chapter two, hear dominion as the responsibility of a steward: ruling the way a good king rules, for the good of what's in his care. Francis of Assisi sang of Brother Sun and Sister Water. Leaders in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches have written about care for creation as part of faith, not a hobby beside it. It comes down to two old verbs: serve the ground, and guard it.

Here's the practice: picking up what isn't yours. Settle, and breathe. Picture a place you pass every day: a sidewalk, a parking lot, a park, the hallway at work or school. See it clearly. Notice the bit of litter you always walk past: a cup, a wrapper, a bag on a fence. Now picture yourself bending down and picking it up, and putting it in the trash or the recycling. Not as a big gesture. As the job given in the garden. If you pray, you can give thanks for that small patch of earth. The bell holds the time.
Tending the garden. Creation care, from Genesis 2:15: the human placed in Eden to dress it and keep it, to serve the earth and guard it.
Your line: till and keep. Today, pick up one piece of litter that isn't yours, in the place you pictured. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Christians practice creation care through church gardens, cleanups, energy and waste changes in congregations, and prayers for creation; some churches keep a Season of Creation each year, and Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant leaders have written on care for the earth.

notes: The carry 'till and keep' follows the index; the KJV of Genesis 2:15 reads 'dress it and to keep it' (Genesis 3:23 has 'to till the ground'). The script explains the carry through the verbs; confirm.

Hebrew verbs: עָבַד ('avad: work, serve; also used of worship) and שָׁמַר (shamar: keep, guard; used of keeping commandments). Lexical claims stated as fact; confirm. Original: לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ and pronunciation; confirm.
Hook: 'the second chapter of the Bible' refers to Genesis 2; the job framing is the narrator's reading of the text, since chapter 1 already gives humans a charge. Confirm.
'Some readers once took dominion as permission to use things up' is a hedged reference to a modern critique of Christian readings of Genesis 1:28; confirm fair.

'Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant leaders have all written about care for creation' (e.g. Pope Francis's Laudato si', Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, Protestant statements) is unnamed and undated; confirm.
howItsDone mentions a Season of Creation kept by some churches; confirm.
